title: Freundlich adsorption of acetic acid on charcoal: from a pH reading to the constant k
summary: Weigh acetic acid into 50 mL of water, shake it with charcoal and watch a third of the molecules stick to the surface while the total never changes, then turn a pH reading into the equilibrium concentration and read the Freundlich constant off the log-log plot.
subject: Chemistry
subtopics: Adsorption from solution onto a solid
Freundlich isotherm and its logarithmic form
Slope and intercept of the log-log plot
concepts: Adsorption is a surface process, so nothing leaves the flask - the adsorbate only changes address
A pH reading gives the hydrogen ion, not the weak acid that produced it
Ka is the conversion factor between [H+] and the concentration of an undissociated weak acid
The C in the Freundlich isotherm is the concentration left at equilibrium, never the initial one
Taking logarithms turns a power law into a straight line whose gradient is 1/n and whose intercept is log k
formulas: weak acid: Ka = [H+]^2 / C, so C = [H+]^2 / Ka
x = mass taken - mass left in solution

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: the mole calculation, the Ka inversion, the mass balance, the slope-to-n step and the final division were all fixed independently
The Ka route checked in both directions: forwards it gives C = 0.10 mol/L from pH 3.00, and substituting back, [H+] = sqrt(Ka x C) = 1.000e-3, reproducing the meter reading exactly

Conservation checked explicitly to machine precision: 0.30 g left in solution + 0.15 g adsorbed = 0.45 g weighed out, and the simulation enforces the same identity frame by frame while the flask is shaking
Two independent routes to k agree: dividing (x/m) by C gives 1.5, and the intercept of the log-log line gives log10 k = 0.176091, i.e. k = 1.500000
Units confirmed by dimensional analysis: (g/g) / (mol/L) = L/mol, which is the unit the question asks for - itself a check that x was correctly taken as a mass rather than a number of moles

The traps reproduced deliberately: using the initial 0.15 M gives exactly 1.0; treating pH 3 as the acid concentration gives an absurd 150; dividing by 50 instead of 0.050 L gives 0.00015; putting x in moles gives 0.025 L/g. None is 1.5

The intended approximation quantified rather than assumed: solving the weak-acid equilibrium exactly, without treating the acid left in solution as wholly undissociated, gives C = 0.1010 mol/L and k = 1.455 - a 3.0% shift. The question's round numbers are chosen so the standard approximation lands on a clean 1.5, which is the intended answer

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which follows the same steps and reports the same intermediate values (1e-3 M, 0.10 M, 0.005 mol, 0.30 g, 0.15 g, n = 1) and the same answer, 1.5 L/mol. IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable at the time of writing

interactivity: Four benches, one per decision the question hides, each gated behind a prediction the student must commit to before the apparatus will settle anything

Laboratory bench drawn as a scene: a digital balance whose display counts up to 0.45 g, a 50 mL measuring cylinder that empties as the water is poured, and a conical flask that fills and then shows the acid dispersing through it
The mole calculation reveals one line at a time as the corresponding action is performed, rather than arriving as a finished block
The volume conversion is a choice, not a given: the student picks between dividing by 50 and by 0.050 L, and the wrong one is refused with the 0.00015 it actually produces
Charcoal grains drawn as irregular porous particles, with 45 acid molecules moving through the liquid, bouncing off the grains and snapping onto surface sites as adsorption proceeds
The flask rocks and the liquid surface sways while shaking, and the animation stops itself the moment equilibrium is reached
Live tally of acid in solution, acid on the charcoal and the total - the total is held at 0.45 g every frame, which is what settles the conservation claim
Digital pH meter whose probe descends into the flask and whose reading settles from 7 down to 3.00 with a little noise before locking
Six-step chemist's reasoning card that walks from the meter reading through [H+], the dissociation equilibrium and the Ka approximation to the equilibrium concentration
Animated mass-balance bar that splits the 0.45 g into the 0.30 g still dissolved and the 0.15 g on the surface, with the arithmetic written underneath
Interactive log-log plot of the Freundlich isotherm with a slope slider: the line pivots about the measured point and the student has to set the gradient the question describes
Animated slope triangle reporting rise, run and rise/run, so 1/n is read off rather than recalled
The intercept marked at log C = 0 and labelled log k, giving a second, independent route to the same answer
A concentration switch that lets the student deliberately build the commonest wrong answer - k = 1.0 from the initial 0.15 M - and be told which quantity the isotherm actually needs
Experiment / Explain toggle that overlays short conceptual notes on every bench without leaving the experiment
Seven expandable JEE traps, each phrased as the misconception a student actually holds, starting with the initial-concentration error
Progressive four-level hint system on every bench, conceptual clue first and near-solution last
Progress bar, four earnable badges and an end-of-lab celebration reporting evidence collected and prediction accuracy
Lab notebook written as the student works, plus a final record table that fills in quantity by quantity and ends at k
Auto play that walks the whole investigation, pausing at each prediction
Teacher mode with objectives, the expected wrong answers ranked by frequency, a teaching order and a discussion question
Answer gated until all four benches have been run, with a reveal-anyway escape
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log
